unit.unitOverview: Say what always happens, not just what happened today: if you heat ice, it melts. State a plain fact about a machine, a material or a place. Use it and there when nothing is doing the action: It takes an hour. There is no signal. Read a notice on a machine, then write and say the steps yourself.

visual.lectureScript:
Hello. This is Unit 11.
This unit is about what always happens.
Not today. Not tomorrow. Every time.
If you press this button, the light comes on.
That is true on Monday, and it is true at night.
First, if and when.
Put if at the front, then say the result.
If you heat ice, it melts.
If you pull the plug out, the screen goes dark.
Both parts are present simple. There is no will here.
Will points at one moment. A thing that is always true has no one moment.
Say if, then the thing you do, then a comma, then the result.
When means the same in these sentences.
When you heat metal, it gets hot.
Use when for something that really does happen.
Use if for something that may happen and may not.
Here is a test you can use on your own.
Put every time at the front of the sentence.
Every time you heat ice, it melts. That works.
So the present simple is right, twice.
You can also turn the sentence round.
Ice melts if you heat it.
The result comes first, then if. No comma this way.
Second, the plain fact.
You do not always need if.
Metal gets hot. Water freezes at zero degrees. The shop opens at nine.
These are facts. They are true before you say them.
Remember the s for he, she and it.
Water freezes. Heat increases the pressure. The fan spins.
Do not say water freeze. Say water freezes.
For a fact that is not true, use does not.
Oil does not dissolve in water.
And ask with does.
Does salt dissolve in cold water? How long does the battery last?
The s sits on does, and only there.
Third, it and there.
Sometimes nobody is doing the action.
But English still needs a word in front of the verb.
Use it for time, distance, weather and temperature.
It takes an hour by bus. It is ten degrees in here.
It is a long way to the station.
Use there is and there are to say that something exists.
There is no signal in this building.
There are two sockets behind the desk.
One thing takes there is. Two or more take there are.
Here is the mistake to watch for.
It is easy to drop the subject.
Not is raining. Say it is raining.
Not is no signal. Say there is no signal.
Many languages do not need a word there. English always does.
Now the words.
Thirty of them, in four groups.
Machines and power: battery, charge, plug, socket, screen, button, signal, wire.
What it does: pump, cool, dissolve, freeze, melt, burn, flow, spin.
Cause and result: cause, result, effect, depend, affect, produce, increase, reduce.
And the ones that go with it and there: distance, temperature, weight, pressure, speed, depth.
In this unit you read a notice for a drinks machine.
You find the rule you need in it.
You write five steps for a machine you know, with a warning.
Then you say those steps out loud and listen back.
Take one card at a time. Say every line.
Let us start.

readings.title: The Phone at the Bus Stop
readings.genre: A short account of one cold morning
readings.setting: A bus stop between two tall buildings, early in the morning.
readings.passageScript:
It is cold this morning, and you are waiting at the bus stop.
You take out your phone. The screen is dark.
You press the button. Nothing happens.
This is not a broken phone. It is the cold.
If the temperature drops, a battery loses power faster.
Every battery does this. Yours is not special.
Hold the phone in both hands for two minutes.
Then press the button again. The screen lights up.
There is something else this morning. There is no signal.
The bus stop stands between two tall buildings.
A thick wall reduces the signal, and here there are two of them.
If you walk to the corner, the signal comes back.
So you have two rules for a cold morning.
Keep the phone warm, and stand where the sky is open.
On the bus you charge the phone from a socket under the seat.
It takes an hour to fill it, and the journey takes forty minutes.
So you arrive with a phone that is almost full.
None of this is luck.
A machine does the same thing every time.
When you know what a machine always does, you stop guessing.

readings.title: What a Kettle Does
readings.genre: A plain explanation of how one machine works
readings.setting: A kitchen, at any time of day.
readings.passageScript:
A kettle is a simple machine, and it does the same thing every time.
Inside, at the bottom, there is a short metal wire.
When you push the plug in and press the switch, power flows along that wire.
The wire gets hot, and the water round it gets hot too.
If you heat water to one hundred degrees, it boils.
Hot air then comes off the top of the water.
Then the kettle stops on its own.
It does not boil all morning.
The hot air touches a small part near the top.
That part switches the power off.
So the kettle does two jobs.
It heats the water, and it watches the water for you.
How long does it take? That depends on three things.
It depends on the weight of the water inside.
It depends on the temperature of the water when you start.
And it depends on the power of the kettle itself.
Cold water and a full kettle take the longest.
One rule is always true.
If the kettle is empty, do not switch it on.
With no water round it, the wire gets far too hot, and it burns.
Every machine in this unit works in the same plain way.
One cause, one result, every time.

readings.title: Notice: The Drinks Machine
readings.setting: The wall beside a drinks machine in a waiting room.
readings.passageScript:
NOTICE
THE DRINKS MACHINE
Waiting room, next to the desk

HOW TO USE IT
1. Look at the screen. If the screen is dark, the machine is off. Tell the desk.
2. Press the button beside the drink you want.
3. The price comes up on the screen.
4. Put the money in the hole under the screen.
5. Take your cup from the open part at the bottom.

PRICES
Tea: 2
Coffee: 3
Water: 1

PLEASE READ THIS
If you press two buttons together, the machine stops and keeps your money.
The cup is hot. Hold it at the top.
If the machine takes your money and gives you nothing, leave a note at the desk.
There is no way to pay with a card. This machine takes money only.
The machine is cleaned every Tuesday at seven in the morning.
It is off for one hour.
If the water is warm and not hot, something is wrong. Do not use it. Tell the desk.

grammar.title: If you heat ice, it melts
grammar.explanation:
Some things happen every time, not only today.
For these, use if or when, and the present simple in both parts.
If you heat ice, it melts.
There is no will here. Nothing in this sentence is a guess about tomorrow.

If you pull the plug out, the screen goes dark.
If the temperature drops below zero, water freezes.
If you stir it, the sugar dissolves faster.

when means the same in these sentences:
When you heat metal, it gets hot.
When the battery is flat, the phone stops.

Turn it round, and the comma goes:
Ice melts if you heat it.
The light comes on when you press this button.

Both parts are present simple, so keep the s:
it melts, it comes, it gets, water freezes.

The test: put every time at the front.
Every time you heat ice, it melts.
That works, so it is always true.
grammar.workedExample:
Two facts: you pull the plug out, and the screen goes dark.
1. Which one do you do? You pull the plug out. That is the if part.
2. Put if at the front: If you pull the plug out
3. Add a comma.
4. Add the result in the present simple: the screen goes dark.
5. If you pull the plug out, the screen goes dark.
6. Check: Every time you pull the plug out, the screen goes dark. Yes, that is true.
grammar.commonMistake:
It is easy to put will in the second part.
No: If you heat ice, it will melt.
Yes: If you heat ice, it melts.
Will points at one moment. A thing that is true every time has no one moment.
Keep the comma when if comes first: If you press it, the light comes on.
grammar.memoryTip: Swap if for every time. If the line still makes sense, use the present simple twice.
grammar.practice:

4. If you stir the salt, it (dissolve) ______ faster.
5. When the temperature drops below zero, water (freeze) ______ .
6. Join these with if: You pull the wire out. The screen goes dark.
7. Turn this round so the result comes first: If you charge it for an hour, it is full.
8. One line is wrong. Fix it: If you burn bread, it will taste bad.
grammar.answerKey:
1. melts
2. does not work
3. spins
4. dissolves
5. freezes
6. If you pull the wire out, the screen goes dark.
7. It is full if you charge it for an hour.
8. If you burn bread, it tastes bad.
The likeliest wrong answer is 8 left as it is, because will sounds right after if. Ask yourself: does this happen every time? If it does, take will out.
Watch 7 too: with the result first, there is no comma.
6 or more right: go on. 5 or fewer: read the rule again, one line at a time.

grammar.title: Metal gets hot: a fact, not just today
grammar.explanation:
You do not always need if.
A present simple sentence can state a fact on its own.
Metal gets hot. Water freezes at zero degrees. The shop opens at nine.
This is not what you did today. It is what is true.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
A fact about a thing:
Metal gets hot.
Ice melts in a warm room.
A thick wall reduces the signal.

A fact about a machine:
This machine spins for three minutes.
The screen goes dark after one minute.
The battery lasts one day.

One thing takes s, like he and she:
water freezes, heat increases, the fan spins.

Not true? Use does not, and the s moves:
Oil does not dissolve in water.
The lamp does not work without a plug.

Ask with does, and the s moves again:
Does salt dissolve in cold water?
How long does the battery last?
grammar.workedExample:
You want to say that salt goes into water and disappears.
1. What is the thing? Salt.
2. Is this true every time, or only today? Every time. So use the present simple.
3. Salt is one thing, like he or she, so the verb takes s: dissolves.
4. Salt dissolves in water.
5. Now make a question with does: Does salt dissolve in water?
6. The s has moved onto does, so the main verb is dissolve again.
grammar.commonMistake:
It is easy to drop the s: Water freeze at zero.
English needs it here: Water freezes at zero.
And it is easy to keep the s in a question: Does it dissolves?
Only one word carries it: Does it dissolve?
grammar.memoryTip: One thing, one s. He, she, it, water, the battery: they all take s.
grammar.practice:

5. Make a question: the battery / last / how long?
6. Make a question: salt / dissolve / in cold water?

8. Write one fact about a machine you use. Use the present simple.
grammar.answerKey:
1. boils
2. reduces
3. does not dissolve
4. produces
5. How long does the battery last?
6. Does salt dissolve in cold water?
7. Ice melts in a warm room.
8. Your own answer. For example: My kettle boils in two minutes.
The likeliest wrong answer is 5 or 6 written as How long does the battery lasts? The s sits on does, and only there.
6 or more right: go on. 5 or fewer: read the rule and do 1 to 4 again.

grammar.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
grammar.title: It takes an hour. There is no signal.
grammar.explanation:
Sometimes nobody is doing the action.
English still needs a word in front of the verb.
Use it for time, distance, weather and temperature.
Use there is and there are to say that something exists.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
it, for time and distance:
It takes an hour by bus.
It is a long way to the station.
It takes twenty minutes on foot.

it, for weather and temperature:
It is cold in here.
It is twenty degrees outside.
It is raining.

there is and there are, for what exists:
There is no signal in this building.
There is a button under the screen.
There are two sockets behind the desk.

One thing: there is. Two or more: there are.

Saying no:
It does not take long.
There is no signal. There are no sockets here.

Asking:
How long does it take?
Is there a socket near the door?
grammar.workedExample:
You want to say that the journey is one hour long.
1. Who or what is doing it? Nobody. An hour is not a person.
2. So start with It.
3. It takes an hour.
4. Now you want to say that the room has no socket.
5. Nothing is doing the action here either. The socket exists, or it does not.
6. So start with There: There is no socket in this room.
7. One socket takes there is. Two sockets take there are.
grammar.commonMistake:
It is easy to drop the subject and say Is raining, or Is no signal.
Many languages do not need a word there. English always does.
Yes: It is raining. There is no signal.
Watch the pair as well: There is one socket. There are two sockets.
grammar.memoryTip: No person and no thing doing it? Start the sentence with It or There.
grammar.practice:

2. ______ no signal inside this building.
3. ______ two buttons under the screen.
4. ______ is ten degrees in here this morning.
5. ______ a plug in the box.
6. Ask how long the journey is. Use it.
7. Ask whether the room has a socket. Use there.
8. Fix this line: Is a long way to the station.
grammar.answerKey:
1. It
2. There is
3. There are
4. It
5. There is
6. How long does it take?
7. Is there a socket in this room?
8. It is a long way to the station.
The likeliest wrong answer is 3 written as There is two buttons. Look at the thing that comes after: two buttons is more than one, so it takes There are.
6 or more right: go on. 5 or fewer: read the rule and say each line out loud.

quizzes.options: It is | It has | There are | There is

quizzes.question: ______ two sockets behind the desk.

quizzes.question: How long ______ to charge?

quizzes.question: The notice says the machine takes money only. What does that mean for a person with a card and no money?
quizzes.options: They can pay at the desk instead. | They must press two buttons together. | They cannot buy a drink from this machine. | They should wait until Tuesday morning.

quizzes.question: Which sentence says what happens every time, and is written correctly?
quizzes.options: If you press it, the light will comes on. | If you press it, the light will come on. | If you press it the light comes on. | If you press it, the light comes on.
quizzes.correctAnswer: If you press it, the light comes on.
quizzes.explanation: Two present simple verbs and a comma after the if part. The second option is correct English but it is about one moment, not every time. The third is missing the comma, and the first puts an s after will, which never happens.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
teacherNotes.note: Will after if is the error to expect, and it is not carelessness. Many learners are taught the first conditional first, so will feels like the natural partner of if. The fix that works is the every time test on Pattern 1: if the sentence still makes sense with every time in front of it, will has to go. Practice 6 items 1 and 8 are where this shows up, and the key names the reason rather than just the correction.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
teacherNotes.note: A dropped subject is the second error, and it belongs to this unit because it and there are exactly the words that carry no meaning of their own. Is raining and Is no signal are both complete sentences in many languages. Practice 6 items 2 and 7 are the same mistake twice on purpose, and the key says so, so the learner sees one rule rather than two corrections.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
teacherNotes.note: Every card shows one item worked through before its practice. Every practice has a key with a score line and a named next step. Every speaking task ends with record, listen back and a checklist the learner can see, and Speaking 4 checks itself against Reading 3 rather than against an opinion. If you are helping, sit with the checklist open and let the learner do the counting.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
teacherNotes.note: Two pairs in this word list are easy to confuse and are gated in the quiz. Affect is the doing word and effect is the thing that happens, tested in Quiz 9. Increase and reduce are opposites and are tested against each other in Quiz 8. Learners often also read depend as a fixed phrase, so the word card practice keeps it with on every time: it depends on the weight, on the temperature, on the distance.
